headline: Supermarket freezers hit by cyberattack, temperatures raised to 50°C across Europe, destroying food
summary: A second major cyberattack has targeted supermarket freezers in Belgium and Sweden, raising temperatures to 50°C and destroying millions of dollars worth of food. This follows a similar incident in France just weeks prior.
details: Just weeks after a similar incident in France, a new cyberattack has crippled supermarket chains in Belgium and Sweden. Hackers targeted stores owned by Ahold Delhaize, ICA, and Coop, remotely raising freezer temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius. This rapid defrosting likely destroyed millions of dollars worth of food.

In Belgium, the attack began Sunday night, affecting at least twenty refrigeration units across Delhaize, Carrefour, and Spar supermarkets. The hackers activated the freezers' built-in defrost mode, overriding temperature and time settings, mirroring the previous attack method.

Sabcobel, a refrigeration fitter, stated they are working hard to protect units but physical modifications are required to address the vulnerability. Switching units to a secure internet connection is considered the simplest temporary solution, a measure many customers adopted after the France attack.
Sweden also saw similar disturbances at ICA and Coop stores, with staff seen discarding shopping carts full of spoiled goods. ICA Kvantum expressed sadness and commitment to restoring operations.

This second attack highlights the critical reliance of basic infrastructure on internet connectivity, making it vulnerable to cyberattacks. The increasing frequency of such physical-world intrusions coincides with the proliferation of AI agents in cybersecurity, which can enable less skilled actors to hack with ease.

Hackers targeted stores owned by Ahold Delhaize, ICA, and Coop, remotely raising freezer temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius. This rapid defrosting likely destroyed millions of dollars worth of food.

Sabcobel, a refrigeration fitter, stated they are working hard to protect units but physical modifications are required to address the vulnerability. Switching units to a secure internet connection is considered the simplest temporary solution, a measure many customers adopted after the France attack.

Sweden also saw similar disturbances at ICA and Coop stores, with staff seen discarding shopping carts full of spoiled goods. ICA Kvantum expressed sadness and commitment to restoring operations.
